questions.question: What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ when $\boldsymbol{x} \neq \boldsymbol{y}$?
What distance does the discrete metric assign to two distinct points?
options: All points have distance $0$ from each other
Distinct points are always exactly $1$ unit apart

questions.question: What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(2,5)$?
What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x})$?
Which values can the discrete metric take?
What is true about the discrete metric and $p$-metrics?
options: The discrete metric is equal to every $p$-metric
The discrete metric is strongly equivalent to exactly one $p$-metric
The discrete metric is not a metric
The discrete metric is not strongly equivalent to any of the $p$-metrics

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, what is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}((1,2),(1,3))$?
options: $\sqrt{1}$ only because it is Euclidean distance

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^2$, what is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}((0,0),(0,0))$?
What happens in the discrete metric when two points are very close in the usual Euclidean sense but still distinct?
options: Their discrete distance becomes close to $0$
Their discrete distance equals their Euclidean distance

questions.question: Which conclusion would be false for the discrete metric?
options: The discrete metric is a distance with values $0$ and $1$
The discrete distance between distinct points is $1$
The discrete distance from a point to itself is $0$
The discrete metric is strongly equivalent to a $p$-metric

questions.question: For the discrete metric, which radius boundary is responsible for $B(x,r)$ changing from $\{x\}$ to the whole space?
options: $r=0$, because every point has distance $0$ from $x$.
$r=2$, because no distance can be below $2$.
$r=1$, because points different from $x$ have distance exactly $1$.
There is no boundary; the ball is always $\{x\}$.

questions.question: A student says every discrete-metric open ball is a singleton. Which radius gives an immediate counterexample?
options: No radius can be a counterexample.

questions.question: What determines the value of the discrete metric?
options: The Euclidean distance between the two points.
Whether the two points are equal or distinct.
The angle between the two points.
The dimension of the ambient space only.

questions.question: How far apart are any two distinct points in the discrete metric?
options: A value depending on their coordinates.

questions.question: What does $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=0$ imply?
What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(-3,-3)$?
What is $d_{\mathrm{disc}}((1,2),(3,4))$?
If $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \lt 1$, what must be true?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}$ and $\boldsymbol{y}$ must be real numbers rather than vectors.

questions.question: Why does the discrete metric ignore ordinary closeness between distinct points?
options: It computes ordinary Euclidean distance exactly.
It assigns smaller distances to points with similar coordinates.
All distinct points are assigned the same distance $1$.
It is defined only for equal points.
